entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 66 Is 66:1-24 . The Humble Comforted, the Ungodly Condemned, at the Lord's Appearing: Jerusalem Made a Joy on Earth. This closing chapter is the summary of Isaiah's prophecies as to the last days, hence the similarity of its sentiments with what went before. 1. heaven ... throne ... where is ... house ... ye build-- The same sentiment is expressed, as a precautionary proviso for the majesty of God in deigning to own any earthly temple as His, as if He could be circumscribed by space ( 1Ki 8:27 ) in inaugurating the temple of stone; next, as to the temple of the Holy Ghost ( Ac 7:48 , 49 ); lastly here, as to "the tabernacle of God with men" ( Is 2:2 , 3 ; Eze 43:4 , 7 ; Re 21:3 ). where-- rather, "what is this house that ye are building, &c.--what place is this for My rest?" [Vitringa].

God loathes even the sacrifices of the wicked (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.11">Is 1:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.15.8">Pr 15:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.28.9">28:9</reference>).<div eID="gen16721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16722" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is as if--</hi>Lowth not so well omits these words: "He that killeth an ox (presently after) murders a man" (as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.39">Eze 23:39</reference>). But the omission in the Hebrew of "is as if"--increases the force of the comparison. Human victims were often offered by the heathen.<div eID="gen16722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16723" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dog's neck--</hi>an abomination according to the Jewish law (<reference osisRef="Deut.23.18">De 23:18</reference>); perhaps made so, because dogs were venerated in Egypt. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9553"/><div sID="gen16732" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9553"/><hi type="bold">5. tremble at ... word--</hi>the same persons as in <reference osisRef="Isa.66.2">Is 66:2</reference>, the believing few among the Jews.<div eID="gen16732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16733" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cast you out for my name's sake--</hi>excommunicate, as if too polluted to worship with them (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.5">Is 65:5</reference>). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9555"/><div sID="gen16738" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9555"/><hi type="bold">7. she--</hi>Zion.<div eID="gen16738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16739" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Before ... travailed ... brought forth--</hi>The accession of numbers, and of prosperity to her, shall be sudden beyond all expectation and unattended with painful effort (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.1">Is 54:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.4.5">4, 5</reference>). Contrast with this case of the future Jewish Church the travail-pains of the Christian Church in bringing forth "a man child" (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.2">Re 12:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.12.5">5</reference>). A man child's birth is in the East a matter of special joy, while that of a female is not so; therefore, it here means the manly sons of the restored Jewish Church, the singular being used collectively for the plural: or the many sons being regarded as one under Messiah, who shall then be manifested as their one representative Head. <div eID="gen16739" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9565"/><div sID="gen16763" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9565"/><hi type="bold">17. in ... gardens--</hi>Hebrew and the Septuagint rather require, "for (entering into) gardens," namely, to sacrifice there [Maurer].<div eID="gen16763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16764" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">behind one tree--</hi>rather, "following one," that is, some idol or other, which, from contempt, he does not name [Maurer]. Vitringa, &c., think the Hebrew for "one," Ahhadh, to be the name of the god; called Adad (meaning One) in Syria (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.17.23">Ac 17:23</reference>). The idol's power was represented by inclined rays, as of the sun shining on the earth. Gesenius translates, "following one," namely, Hierophant ("priest"), who led the rest in performing the sacred rites.<div eID="gen16764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16765" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in ... midst--</hi>namely, of the garden (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.65.3">Is 65:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.65.4">4</reference>).<div eID="gen16765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16766" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mouse--</hi>legally unclean (<reference osisRef="Lev.11.29">Le 11:29</reference>) because it was an idol to the heathen (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.37.36">Is 37:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.4">1Sa 6:4</reference>). Translate, "the field mouse," or "dormouse" [Bochart]. The Pharisees with their self-righteous purifications, and all mere formalists, are included in the same condemnation, described in language taken from the idolatries prevalent in Isaiah's times. <div eID="gen16766" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_plain: 19. sign-- a banner on a high place, to indicate the place of meeting for the dispersed Jewish exiles, preparatory to their return to their land ( Is 5:26 ; 11:12 ; 62:10 ). those that escape of them-- the Gentile survivors spared by God (see on Is 66:18 ; Zec 14:16 ). Is 2:2 , 3 ; Mi 5:7 ; and Zec 14:16-19 represent it, not that the Jews go as missionaries to the Gentiles, but that the Gentiles come up to Jerusalem to learn the Lord's ways there. Tarshish-- Tartessus in Spain, in the west. Pul-- east and north of Africa: probably the same as Philoe, an island in the Nile, called by the Egyptians Pilak, that is, the border country, being between Egypt and Ethiopia [Bochart]. Lud-- the Libyans of Africa ( Ge 10:13 ), Ludim being son of Mizraim (Egypt): an Ethiopian people famous as bowmen ( Jr 46:9 ): employed as mercenaries by Tyre and Egypt ( Eze 27:10 ; 30:5 ). Tubal-- Tibarenians, in Asia Minor, south of the Caucasus, between the Black Sea and Araxes. Or, the Iberians [Josephus]. Italy [Jerome]. Javan-- the Greeks; called Ionians, including all the descendants of Javan, both in Greece and in Asia Minor ( Ge 10:2-4 ). my glory ... Gentiles-- (Mal 1:11).

It cannot mean the mere entrance of the Jews into the Christian Church; for such an entrance would be by faith, not upon "horses, litters, and mules" [Houbigant]. "Offering" is metaphorical, as in Ro 15:16 . horses-- not much used by the Jews. The Gentiles are here represented as using their modes of conveyance to "bring" the Jews to Jerusalem. chariots-- as these are not found in Oriental caravans, translate, "vehicles," namely, borne, not drawn on wheels. litters-- covered sedans for the rich. upon swift beasts-- dromedaries: from Hebrew root, "to dance," from their bounding motion, often accelerated by music [Bochart]. Panniers were thrown across the dromedaries' back for poorer women [Horsley].

navigation_sections.content_plain: CHAPTER 66 Is 66:1-24 . The Humble Comforted, the Ungodly Condemned, at the Lord's Appearing: Jerusalem Made a Joy on Earth. This closing chapter is the summary of Isaiah's prophecies as to the last days, hence the similarity of its sentiments with what went before.
